title: Genomic population structure and local adaptation in the emerging commercially exploited Littorina littorea
content:
Abstract
To address food deficit, stakeholders continuously diversify food systems by exploiting new commercially viable species. However, the absence of sustainable management measures often conflicts with global biodiversity policies. In light of this challenge, understanding genetic diversity and the geographic scale of population connectivity is essential. We employ ddRAD sequencing in Littorina littorea, a low-trophic, emerging commercial species, to investigate its genetic population structure in Norwegian coastal waters. From an initial detection of over two million SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms), 60 831 loci were retained for downstream genomic analyses in 189 individuals sampled across 17 coastal sites. Our results revealed significant isolation-by-distance across the study area, likely reflecting genetic divergence between populations along the west and southern coasts of Norway. While the overall genetic structure appears to be primarily shaped by genetic drift, our genome scan analyses provided evidence for selection acting on specific loci. We identified 39 SNPs potentially under selection, of which 16 overlapped with genes encoding proteins involved in transmembrane transport, metabolic processes, and pathogenesis-related functions. We found no evidence supporting the presence of chromosomal inversions. Oceanographic modelling suggests a likely link between observed genetic divergence and the prevailing ocean current in the region. Our findings demonstrate the adaptive potential of distinct populations to varying environmental conditions and highlight the importance of preserving their full genetic diversity to ensure long-term resilience and sustainability.
